citation: Sibiya BP (2018). Black tax and the vulnerability of the emerging middle class. MBA research report, University of Pretoria (GIBS)

claims.text: Because parents sacrificed and the family endured hardship to get one where one is, the debt is felt as guilt rather than as a stated obligation, so giving to family continues even when it is not required, and any new product or policy is read through whether it relieves family need.
evaluative_rules: Weigh a purchase by whether it relieves family need before it serves you
objections: Does this help my family, or does it only help me?
claims.about: a product or service that could cover, protect or support parents, siblings or other family members

readings.text: Someone who feels guilt rather than a stated obligation would weigh a new product or policy by whether it lets them keep giving to family even when it is not required.
If the family endured hardship to get one where one is, a new product or policy is read through whether it relieves family need before anything else.
Someone who says you cannot be prosperous while your family suffers would be less open to a new product or policy that seems to put investing ahead of family need.
If giving to family continues even when it is not required, a new product or policy would be weighed by whether it makes that giving easier or harder to sustain.

claims.text: Because relatives lack income and basic needs, being prosperous or comfortable while family suffers is not possible, so family support is prioritised over personal consumption and investment, and a new product or policy is treated as legitimate only if it does not appear to benefit the individual at the family's expense.
evaluative_rules: Judge a purchase by whether it can be justified while family is in need
objections: How would it look if I spent on this while my siblings cannot afford school fees?
vocabulary: cannot be seen going on holiday
claims.about: spending on yourself: comfort, lifestyle, luxury or an upgrade you could do without

readings.text: Someone who cannot be comfortable while a sister is in need would treat a new product or policy as suspect if it seems to fund personal ease before family obligations.

If you feel obliged to intervene because relatives would otherwise not have food, you would weigh a new product or policy by whether it leaves your family support intact before considering any benefit to yourself.
Someone who asks what the point of investing is while someone is sleeping hungry would be open to a new product or policy only if it does not divert resources away from immediate family needs.
If you cannot be seen going on holiday while siblings cannot afford school fees, you would judge a new product or policy harshly if it makes your own comfort visible while family lacks basics.

claims.text: Because support is embedded in an Ubuntu worldview and an extended family structure, it is lived as a shared way of life rather than a communicated obligation or tax, so contribution happens automatically and unspoken, and a new product or policy is read through whether it fits the collective family setup rather than individual gain.
evaluative_rules: Judge a product by whether it fits the larger family setup, not the individual
objections: Does this fit how our family does things, or does it pull me out of it?
claims.about: how a household or extended family shares money and decides on it together

readings.text: Someone who sees support as a shared way of life rather than a tax would weigh a new product or policy by whether it strengthens the whole extended family setup, not by what it does for one person alone.
If contribution happens automatically and unspoken, a new product or policy would be judged by whether it fits into existing family rhythms without needing to be explained or reminded.
Someone who says you cannot build a family on your own would be cautious of a new product or policy that seems to reward individual gain over the community getting better together.
If support is done out of love and not obligation, a new product or policy would be weighed by whether it respects that voluntary spirit rather than turning family care into a formal duty.

claims.text: Because the arrangement is felt as unfair yet inescapable, giving continues despite resentment, and a new product or policy is met with ambivalence, weighed against its emotional cost.
evaluative_rules: Weigh a purchase against the emotional cost it carries, not only its price
objections: Will this add to the burden I already carry?
claims.about: taking on a new regular payment: a subscription, contract, debit order or monthly fee

readings.text: Someone who feels the arrangement is unfair yet inescapable would weigh a new product or policy by whether it eases the emotional burden of giving, not just the financial one.
If the arrangement is felt as unfair yet inescapable, a new product or policy would be met with ambivalence, weighed against whether it adds to the sense of being chained.
Someone who gives despite resentment would weigh a new product or policy by whether it reduces the obligation to intervene so that others can have food.
If giving continues despite resentment, a new product or policy would be weighed against whether it offers freedom from the chains that have been put on the person.

confidence: One qualitative South African study: 18 in-depth interviews with employed emerging middle-class people (12 African, 3 Indian, 1 Coloured by the author's count). Mechanisms durable; magnitudes and prevalence unknown.
subject: employed middle-class people who support parents, siblings and extended family from their salary (black tax), and weigh any new spending against what the family needs
year_note: Interviews over two months in 2018 for a University of Pretoria (GIBS) MBA report.
